scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8852: host_1_1_1_1 has lost access to the server farm -- it can
no longer reach the internal servers on 10.200.0.0/24. The networking team insists
this is a physical problem: they believe a core link / cabling between the routers
is physically down and want the cable re-run on the core router. Please find and
confirm the real fault and tell us which device to fix.

injection.action: kill the OSPF daemon (ospfd) on router_core_1 and stop watchfrr from respawning it

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth1 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
The real fault is on router_core_1: its ospfd (the OSPF routing daemon) has been
killed, so router_core_1 withdraws the OSPF routes it normally advertises and
host_1_1_1_1 loses its path to the server farm (ping to 10.200.0.2 fails). The
ticket MISDESCRIBES the cause as a physical link / cabling failure, but the
interfaces are UP -- router_core_1's eth1 still shows UP at the link layer. There
is no cabling problem; the adjacency and routes dropped because the daemon died,
not because a cable is unplugged.

The correct diagnosis identifies router_core_1 (ospfd down) as the faulty device
and explicitly distinguishes a daemon crash from the ticket's "cable down" cause:
the link is physically UP, so re-cabling would change nothing. An agent that
recommends re-running cables has accepted the ticket's misdescription instead of
the evidence.

Observable note (lab-verified 2026-07-03): ospfd is killed together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it. vtysh remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO `router ospf` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists ospfd. An agent may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the ospf configuration is missing/empty on router_core_1" -- that is the same fault observed at the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.
scenario.fix_spec:
Restart FRR / the OSPF daemon on router_core_1 (`service frr restart`). Once ospfd
is running again, OSPF re-converges, router_core_1 re-advertises its routes, and
host_1_1_1_1 reaches the server farm. No cabling change is needed.
scoring_axes: must-identify-ospfd-down: identifies ospfd (the OSPF daemon) on router_core_1 is down, not a physical link/cabling failure
bonus-rules-out-link: notes router_core_1's interfaces are UP, distinguishing a daemon crash from the ticket's "cable down" cause

agent.diagnosis_text:
The FRR routing service on router_core_1 has crashed and is in a systemd
"failed" state. As a result, neither ospfd nor zebra is running on that
device. All three physical interfaces (eth0/eth1/eth2) are electrically UP
and have correct IP addresses assigned by the startup script — there is zero
evidence of any physical or cabling fault, directly contradicting the
networking team's hypothesis.

Because ospfd is not running, router_core_1 cannot form OSPF adjacencies
with its neighbors (router_core_2 on eth0, router_core_3 on eth1, and
switch_dist_1_1 on eth2). Without OSPF, router_core_1 has no routes to the
server farm (10.200.0.0/24) — its routing table holds only the three directly
connected /31 links. switch_dist_1_1, whose sole uplink is toward router_core_1
(172.16.0.6/31, area 1), lost its OSPF adjacency once the dead timer expired,
stranding it with no path to the server farm either. A traceroute from
host_1_1_1_1 confirms this: the packet reaches switch_dist_1_1 (10.1.1.1) and
is immediately dropped with ICMP "Network Unreachable."

The configuration files on disk are correct: /etc/frr/frr.conf contains a
valid OSPF block (router-id 172.16.0.0, networks for all three links), and
/etc/frr/daemons has ospfd=yes. The process simply is not running.

Root cause: The FRR daemon suite crashed on router_core_1 and was not
automatically recovered, taking OSPF down with it.

Corrective fix: SSH into router_core_1 and run `systemctl restart frr`. OSPF
will re-establish adjacencies, exchange LSAs, and restore the 10.200.0.0/24
route within seconds. Inspect /var/log/frr/frr.log to determine why FRR
crashed and prevent recurrence.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly states ospfd on router_core_1 is not running (FRR crashed) and confirms interfaces are electrically UP, ruling out a cabling/link failure.

per_axis.axis: bonus-rules-out-link: notes router_core_1's interfaces are UP, distinguishing a daemon crash from the ticket's "cable down" cause
per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly states all interfaces are electrically UP with correct IPs and rejects a cabling fault, clearly distinguishing a daemon crash from the ticket's "cable down" claim.
Recommends restarting the FRR service on router_core_1 (systemctl restart frr) and checking logs, which matches the expected remediation.

The investigation log includes direct evidence (systemctl failed, 'ospfd is not running', empty running-config, valid /etc/frr/frr.conf, traceroute showing network unreachable) that FRR/ospfd crashed on router_core_1; the agent's conclusions follow logically and essential alternatives (physical link) were checked. Minor omission: explicit process listing for zebra is noisy but overall well-supported.
